title: Training Generalizable Collaborative Agents via Strategic Risk Aversion
claim: Moderate conservatism improves equilibrium outcomes, and sufficient conservatism eliminates free-riding, as theory predicts.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared risk-aversion x-axis, double-headed arrow marking gap δ
description: Two side-by-side line plots, each with a single thick blue curve on a white background, labeled (i) and (ii). Both share an x-axis, the risk-aversion level τ from 0 to 2, with arrows marking less versus more risk-averse. Panel (i) plots equilibrium utility U_i against τ. The curve rises to a peak near τ=1, at the C−1/10 gridline, then falls to C−1/8 at τ=2. A horizontal line at C−1/3 marks the baseline utility at τ=0. Panel (ii) plots the probability of cooperating against τ. A pitchfork-style bifurcation appears: upper and lower branches converge at τ≈0.8 and merge into a nearly flat middle branch. A black double-headed arrow labeled δ marks the gap between branches. The eye goes first to the arched curve in panel (i).
caption: (i). Expected utility of each player as a function of the degree of risk aversion $\tau$ at equilibrium, when $\epsilon=1$ in [ref]. Player's utilities can first increase with risk aversion before decreasing due to over-conservatism, meaning that strategic risk aversion can yield better performing equilibria than Nash or QRE. (ii). Probability that a player collaborates at a RQE as a function of the level of risk aversion, for $\epsilon=0.2$ for the game in Example [ref]. Strategic risk aversion alleviates free riding entirely after a given threshold (i.e., $\delta \rightarrow 0$) as our theory predicts.
abstract: Many emerging agentic paradigms require agents to collaborate with one another (or people) to achieve shared goals. Unfortunately, existing approaches to learning policies for such collaborative problems produce brittle solutions that fail when paired with new partners. We attribute these failures to a combination of free-riding during training and a lack of strategic robustness. To address these problems, we study the concept of strategic risk aversion and interpret it as a principled inductive bias for generalizable cooperation with unseen partners. While strategically risk-averse players are robust to deviations in their partner's behavior by design, we show that, in collaborative games, they also (1) can have better equilibrium outcomes than those at classical game-theoretic concepts like Nash, and (2) exhibit less or no free-riding. Inspired by these insights, we develop a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithm that integrates strategic risk aversion into standard policy optimization methods. Our empirical results across collaborative benchmarks (including an LLM collaboration task) validate our theory and demonstrate that our approach consistently achieves reliable collaboration with heterogeneous and previously unseen partners across collaborative tasks.
